extracted.intended_audience: general readers / SNL fans / pop-culture readers
extracted.subtask_description: A listicle-style article describing notable Saturday Night Live cast members who were fired and the reasons or circumstances behind their departures. It collects examples that illustrate causes of dismissal (on-air mistakes, politics, fit, budget, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Racist or homophobic public statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly expressed racist and homophobic statements in a performer’s act or podcast that become known to the show or public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shane Gillis was fired before ever performing after SNL learned of routinely racist and homophobic statements he’d made. The piece highlights the role of vetting and how offensiveness—especially when it intersects with representation on the cast (e.g., an openly gay Asian castmate)—can prompt immediate dismissal and public statements condemning the behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uttering profanity / violating broadcast taboos live
rubrics_metrics.description: Using profanity or otherwise breaking network broadcast taboos on live television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Charles Rocket’s on-air f-bomb (Feb. 21, 1981) and Jenny Slate’s accidental use of “fucking” instead of “frigging” are cited as incidents that precipitated or contributed to dismissal. The article notes context matters (seasonal turmoil, producer tolerance) and that such incidents can be treated differently depending on other factors (e.g., overall season stability, prior standing with producers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not 'clicking' / poor fit with the show’s style
rubrics_metrics.description: Being talented but failing to integrate into SNL’s particular sketch style or failing to connect with writers/producers so that sketches don’t land or get produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Sarah Silverman, Jenny Slate, Ann Risley, Gilbert Gottfried and others cited as ‘never clicking’ or not making an impression. The article emphasizes that performers whose ideas or style don’t fit the show often see their sketches killed (or never aired) and can be let go without a catastrophic on-air incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going off script / improvisation that derails sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Departing from the written lines or performing unexpected material that disrupts the sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damon Wayans was fired after using an unexpected stereotypical accent that derailed a sketch; Lorne Michaels’ reaction was immediate and severe. The article frames this as a serious rule at SNL — spontaneous departures that damage a sketch can lead to instant dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage fright / visible performance errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Nervousness or a visible performance meltdown during a live sketch that undermines the performer’s effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jenny Slate’s stage fright in her first sketch, where she visibly faltered and used the wrong word, is given as an example; although producers may console performers, such moments can contribute to being let go if the performer otherwise doesn’t fit or recover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of airtime / being overshadowed in a large, star-filled cast
rubrics_metrics.description: Not being given screen time or featured moments because other cast members dominate sketches or because the cast is too large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rob Riggle and Sarah Silverman are cited as examples: in massive casts performers can struggle to get a foothold ('drinking out of a fire hose'), and insufficient airtime/visibility can lead to not being rehired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network/producer politics and executive meddling
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions by network executives or political interference (e.g., executive preferences, external pressure) that result in firings irrespective of on-air talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Don Ohlmeyer’s influence in the firings of Adam Sandler and Chris Farley and his campaign against Norm Macdonald. It notes external meddling, network relationships, and executive tastes can override creative considerations and lead to cast changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget cuts and financial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fires or non-renewals motivated by budgetary constraints, contract buyouts, or cost-cutting measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chris Parnell’s (and others’) dismissals are attributed to budget cuts; the piece explains that producers sometimes remove performers to reduce payroll or because they cannot afford to buy out as many contracts, making financials a practical criterion for cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal problems / substance abuse concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal issues such as substance abuse that affect a performer’s reliability, health, or the show’s risk tolerance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chris Farley’s substance problems are discussed as a factor in his ouster and how Michaels used employment status to encourage rehab. The article notes that personal trouble can prompt intervention and, ultimately, dismissal if it threatens the show or the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disputes with producers or calling out the show
rubrics_metrics.description: Openly criticizing the show, its diversity, or its leadership in ways that create friction with decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay Pharoah’s history of calling out SNL’s lack of diversity is mentioned as having put him at risk and possibly contributing to his later firing. The piece suggests speaking out can have career consequences within the show’s power dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholesale cast resets under new leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new producer or leadership change seeks to remake the show’s cast and writing staff, leading to mass firings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dick Ebersol’s post-Jean Doumanian cleanup of Season 6 and Lorne Michaels’ later reboots are cited; entire casts and writing staffs can be replaced when leadership wants to 'start over,' making tenure vulnerable to managerial change rather than individual failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted retaliation tied to jokes about executives’ associates
rubrics_metrics.description: When a performer’s material mocks or targets close associates/friends of powerful executives, leading to targeted adverse actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm Macdonald’s jokes about O.J. Simpson—an associate of NBC executive Don Ohlmeyer—are cited as part of a campaign that led to his demotion and eventual firing. The article frames this as an example where interpersonal relationships and offended executives can precipitate dismissal.
